title: The Small Finds and Vessel Glass from Insula VI.1 Pompeii. Excavations 1995-2006
description:
The aim of this work is to put into the public domain the small finds and the vessel glass recovered from excavations in Insula VI.1 Pompeii which ran from 1995 to 2006. At the time these were known as the Anglo-American Project in Pompeii (AAPP), and were run as a summer school by the Universities of Bradford and Oxford. The aim of the excavations was to uncover the development of the insula prior to the destruction of the town in AD 79. The excavations produced a very large body of material ranging in date from the second century BC to the final years of Pompeii's existence. The report is in two parts. A letterpress volume provides a full, illustrated discussion of the finds. The digital part provides the full database to allow others to further interrogate the data

Work with the archive has enabled the changes in in what people chose to use over the important late Republican and early Imperial period. The growth in the absolute amount consumed, as well as an ever widening range of specialist products, is demonstrated. There is a considerable amount of data relating to the Augustan consumer boom, and there is also evidence for other major changes taking place in the last decade or so of the town's life. Topics considered include the nature of textile working, the rise in the use of perfumes, and the growth of leisure activities.  The assemblage is particularly useful for exploring the growth of glass vessel use, and the impact of the arrival of blown vessels.. It will be of interest both to finds specialists and those with a wider interest in the economy and changing lifestyles of this formative period.
creator: H. E. M. Cool

title: Copper alloy FURNITURE FITTING
description:
A copper alloy zoomorphic furniture fitting or vessel mount of probable post medieval to modern date (c. AD 1650 - 1900). The fitting is in the shape of an animal's paw and exhibits four moulded toes, each of which terminates in a pointed claw. The foot is most likely to be of a lion, or other big cat. The foot has an S-shaped profile and tapers into a flat oval plate at the top. The corroded remains of a copper alloy shank are visible projecting from the top of the plate. The edge of the plate exhibits an incomplete perforation or rivet hole for attachment to the bottom of an object such as a box or casket. The reverse of the fitting is hollow. The fitting is heavily corroded and has an uneven mottled greeen patina.
Furniture fittings of this type are extremely difficult to date due to the fact that this type of fitting retains its popularity from the Roman period to the modern. Many similar examples of the type of fitting have been found at Pompeii, manufactured in both copper-alloy and silver, for example on a large tripod brazier (Ward-Perkins and Claridge, no.209), in a more elaborate form on a candelabrum (ibid no. 141b) on small portable altars and stands (as ibid no. 213, 211), all made from bronze, and on circular silver stands on which stood small silver dishes (as ibid no. 320). In all these examples the entire object is made of metal, the foot soldered to the body of the object. A silver example, exhibiting a different attachment method to the examples from Pompeii was found during excavations at Piddington Roman villa and is recorded on this database as: NARC-081A11.
The method of attachment on the example discussed here differs both from those from Pompeii and from the Piddington example. A comparison with other examples recorded on the database (see below) and examples attached to items of furniture suggests that this example is more likely to be a post medieval or modern fitting copying the Roman form.
Similar examples on the database include: SUR-A6F0F5,  NARC-4C9C98, WAW-56B281 & IOW-64B919. 
The fitting measures 18.38mm in height, 19.33mm maximum width, 6.37mm minimum width, is 7.74mm thick and weighs 7.85g.

title: Copper alloy STYLUS
description:
The object is possibly a Roman stylus made from cast copper alloy. 
    
    In plan it is an elongated triangular shape, with slightly concave sides. The tip is broken, but this is not a recent break. Just below the break there is a linear horizontal groove as decoration on one face. 
    
    In profile the stylus tapers from the most narrow break edge to the base edge. This base edge is very fine. The stylus is not flat in profile, but is slightly convex, which is slightly irregular, which may indicate it occurred during use and not design. 
    
    The stylus has a mid blue/green coloured patina. It measures 26.4mm long, 12.9mm wide and 1.6mm thick. It weighs 1.09g.
    
   Hattatt illustrates a very similar shaped stylus terminal in plan from Pompeii, however in profile Hattatt's is thicker at the neck, and along the blade.

title: Iron ANVIL
description:
An incomplete, wrought iron, Roman, probable, anvil, AD.43-450. The object comprises a cuboid block of iron, the top surface appears slightly domed from repeated striking. The sides appear to be fairly parallel, though there is a slight taper from the top to the bottom.. The object has a fairly even dark black patina with patches of orange oxidation. The sides of the anvil are pitted, probably from corrosion after deposition.
The object can be compared to A1 in Manning's catalogue, (1976:Pl 1) though it lacks the lower wedge for connecting it to a block. Manning states that flat based anvils are not unknown from the Roman world, with examples from Pompeii (1976, 1).
The object can be compared to SF-614293 on the PAS database which dates to a similar period. Both have comparable weights above 20 Kg.

title: Pompeian Plasters Database
description: The study presented in this database concerns plasters used for wall decorations in Pompeii. Earlier experiences in the field showed that plasters compositions change over time. The hypothesis for the study was that there is a connection between the typology and the relative chronology in which the plasters appear on the walls, and that these factors are related not only in single houses or quarters but over the site. The variations were assumed to be related to technology, craftsmanship and fashion. Focus has been set on materials and styles. The database has three sections: Houses, Samples and Types. The types are sorted according to the system of types which is 0 (Zero), which contains the earliest plasters identified, the chronologically namned A-H and the additional X, a group that contains other kinds of materials, such as cocciopesto, modern restoration materials, or waterproof plaster, just to mention some.

title: Ceramic FLUE TILE
description:
An irregular fragment of a Roman box flue tile.
The piece is of flat section and orange-brown in colour. The outer surface is decorated by a roller-printed pattern in which two areas of chevrons border a band that contains what appear to be the letters 'IX', with the 'X' being incomplete.
Length: 99.9 mm; width: 67.7 mm; thickness: 14.3 mm. Weight: 123.48 g.
Similar chevron designs can be seen on a box flue tile from London (Brodribb 1987: 110), but no exact parallel could be found for this pattern. The possible letters may be tally marks relating to the counting of batches of tiles; however, where these occur, they are usually scored rather than moulded (ibid. 131-135), and it is probable that these marks are simply an element of the tile's design. Evidence from excavations at Pompeii and elsewhere suggests box flue tiles were invented in the 1st century AD (ibid. 71).

title: Copper alloy MEDALLION
description:
A cast copy of a copper-alloy medallion of Marcus Aurelius as Caesar (AD 138-61), struck at 'Rome' AD 155-6 (Reece Period 7).
Obverse: AVRELIVS CAESAR AVG PII FIL TR P X COS II; Bare-headed and draped right
Reverse: Anepigraphic: Minerva standing left with shield behind, holding out right hand towards Vulcan seated right, holding thunderbolt.  Between them, anvil on pedestal.
cf. Gnecchi, I Medaglioni Romani, volume 2, p.35 (pl. 65, no. 3)
This medallion is cast from a specimen in Naples Museum, Italy (no. 15997) - information kindly supplied by prof. Dr. Franz Mittag at the University of Cologne in Germany.
Most cast copies of medallions were made in the early modern period and it is tempting to suggest that this medallion was collected on a Grand Tour in Naples where many people visited to see the sites of Pompeii and Herculaneum.  There still remains the mystery of how this piece ended up in the archaeological record where it did.

title: Copper alloy FURNITURE FITTING
description:
A cast copper-alloy furniture fitting, probably of Roman date, c. AD 43-410.
The fitting is discoidal, with a rounded boss with a projecting hollow cylinder emerging from its centre on the upper face. The reverse also has a hollow cylindrical projection, but emerging beneath the outer edges of the boss on the upper face. Iron corrosion obscures details on the outer disc of the fitting, but the underside reveals an iron nail with a square shank bent against the cylindrical projection, and the base of three more nail shafts, for a total of at least four nails placed regularly around the circumference of the disc, though there is a gap where there is no evidence for nails.
From the shape of the fitting, it appears that the reverse was slotted into a larger piece of furniture over a rod that emerged from the front or upper face. The fitting was then nailed into position.
The shape of the object is consistent in shape with furniture fittings visible on Roman folding tripods and chairs (for example, from Pompeii), though this could be from another item of furniture.

title: Copper alloy STEELYARD WEIGHT
description:
A copper-alloy and lead Roman steelyard weight. The weight a head weight in the form of a double head. On the top of the heads is a suspension loop and the bottom of the weight is flat. Both faces at distinctly different in form. The larger head is more pronounced, projects further forward and has more distinct features. Both eyes are deeply sunken, the nose is large and bulbous and the lips of the mouth clearly defined. The second face is flatter and worn. The eyes are just about perceptible but the nose and mouth are very worn. There is a slight beard still visible and large tufts of hair on the sides of the head. The two faces opposite each other could represent the Roman God Janus. However, the crudeness of the weight makes this unclear. The weight is insular in style and probably copying a similar to a double weight from Pompeii (Franken 1994, Aequiponia, pg.169, No.B58).
The weight is slightly under the mass of 1 Roman ounce but this is to be expected with such a crudely made and worn weight.
